_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Why do I need “the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam”? From that [general ruling about the whole chapter] you already learn that the halakha follows him, since the Rabbis do not disagree with him.
rashi:a2.1: Had he said “the halakha follows the whole chapter” and not said [the ruling] below, “the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei,” I would have said that “the halakha throughout the whole chapter” refers to Rabbi Yosei.
rashi:a2.2: And what is “throughout the whole chapter,” which implies a lot? Because Rabbi Yosei said two things in the mishna: “he clears space for the cleaver,” and “likewise he plucks the hair to see the place of the blemish.” But [I would say] Rav did not say it about Rabban Shimon [ben Gamliel], since he said “except where there is a dispute,” and on Rabban Shimon there is a dispute in a baraita, and a dispute in a baraita counts as a dispute. That is why he told us explicitly “the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei”: to reveal and say that this “halakha throughout the whole chapter” refers to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and a dispute in a baraita is not a dispute.
tosafot:a2.1: And a dispute in a baraita is a dispute: And if you ask: then [the Rabbis] must disagree with Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam too in some baraita, whichever way you look at it, since it was necessary to rule that the halakha follows him? One can say: perhaps no dispute is taught, neither in a mishna nor in a baraita, but [Rav] knew by tradition that the Rabbis disagree with him.
rashi:a4.1: Is merciful: it loves the offspring of its fellow [animal].
gershom:a1.1: Because it is merciful: it nurses the offspring of another animal even though it is not its own, and perhaps it has not yet given birth for the first time; as we said, a minority give milk even though they have not given birth. Therefore the one that comes after it is a firstborn out of doubt.
gershom:a2.1: The matter stands in its presumptive status: it is certainly its offspring, and the one that comes after it is exempt.
rashi:a5.1: And found males: those born now hanging on, attached to and nursing from the older ones, which were already exempt from the firstborn; and the females born now he found hanging on the first-time mothers. So now the priest has nothing here: among the males there is no firstborn, since they are the offspring of the older ones; and for the females hanging on the first-time mothers, the law of the firstborn does not apply to them.
rashi:a5.2: He need not be concerned: to be stringent and treat them as uncertain firstborns, saying that perhaps the offspring of this one came to that one, and the males are the offspring of the first-time mothers.
tosafot:a5.1: One who enters amid his flock at night … on the next day he arose …: It is puzzling: why did he need to put it this way? Let him say: one who enters amid his flock and sees males hanging … and females …! One can say that he put it this way to teach a greater novelty: even though their birth certainly took place at night, when the mothers do not yet recognize their offspring, and they tend to err at night so that the offspring of this one comes to that one, even so we are not concerned.
gershom:a3.1: Males hanging: nursing from the older ones, those that are not first-time mothers; and females nursing, hanging on the first-time mothers. He need not be concerned, etc. And all are exempt from the firstborn, since each one nurses from its own mother.
rashi:a6.1: That it is not merciful: toward the offspring of another animal.
rashi:a6.2: Unless it has given birth: if it had offspring at the outset, then for this one, certainly, even if this offspring is not its own, it is exempt from the firstborn, since it had another. But where it has given birth, we are concerned for mercy, that it shows mercy to the offspring of another animal.
gershom:a4.1: That it is not merciful unless it has given birth: this is what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: one that has never given birth is certainly not merciful.
gershom:a5.1: But one that has given birth: is certainly merciful to offspring that is not its own.
gershom:a6.1: Or perhaps: even one that has given birth is not merciful to one that is not its own.
rashi:a7.1: What difference does it make? With regard to the firstborn it is exempt whichever way you look at it, since if this one is not its own, it had another.
rashi:a7.2: To be flogged on its account: for this one trailing after it, because of “it and its offspring.”
rashi:a7.3: He is not flogged: since perhaps it is not its own.
gershom:a7.1: This dilemma matters only with regard to “it and its offspring.” For if we say that an animal that has given birth is merciful, it is exempt from the firstborn whichever way you look at it, since it has already given birth. But with regard to “it and its offspring” one needs to know whether it is its offspring or not, to be flogged on its account if he slaughtered it together with it.
rashi:a8.1: He need not be concerned, etc.: evidently he presumes it is certainly its own, since it is merciful only to its own.
gershom:a8.1: He need not be concerned, etc.: evidently it is not merciful to one that is not its own, and one is flogged on its account because of “it and its offspring.”
rashi:a8.2: Does it teach: “He need not be concerned that perhaps it is the offspring of another”?
rashi:a8.3: It teaches “was”: and this is what it is saying: whichever way you look at it, it is exempt from the firstborn, since one need not be concerned that it is merciful to its fellow’s offspring unless it had another offspring at the outset. Therefore, with regard to the firstborn it is certainly exempt, but with regard to “it and its offspring” it is a matter of doubt.
gershom:a9.1: Does it teach “is”: “lest it is the offspring of another”? Had it taught “is,” it would imply what you said; but since it teaches “was,” this is what it means: he need not, etc.
rashi:a10.1: Perhaps it showed mercy: since all of them have offspring. Rather, evidently, even when it has given birth it is merciful only to its own. And [the Gemara] answers: in a place where its own is present, etc.
gershom:a10.1: In a place where its own is present: it is not merciful to others. But where its own is not present, the question remains.
rashi:a11.1: The matter stands in its presumptive status … and similarly: that is, since the latter clause teaches “And similarly Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would say: One who enters, etc.,” is it not from the latter clause, which teaches “and similarly,” etc.
rashi:a11.2: Certainly its own: each and every one hanging on it is its own, since you said that where its own is present it does not leave its own and show mercy to one that is not its own. The first clause too, which teaches “the matter stands in its presumptive status,” presumes that it is certainly its own, and with regard to “it and its offspring” one is also flogged.
gershom:a11.1: The matter stands in its presumptive status, and similarly he would say, etc.; just as the latter clause is certainly its own: since all of them gave birth.
gershom:a12.1: So too the first clause: “the matter stands in its presumptive status” speaks of where it is certainly its own, and we do not say that if it gave birth it shows mercy to one that is not its own.
rashi:a12.1: This one as it is: the latter clause is certain, the first clause is doubtful.
gershom:a13.1: This one as it is and that one as it is: the latter clause is certainly its own, and the first clause is not certainly its own; rather it may be showing mercy, and one is not flogged for “it and its offspring.”
rashi:a12.2: And what is “and similarly”? Since they are not alike.
rashi:a12.3: And he answers: regarding the exemption, they are alike in this: just as in the latter clause they are certainly exempt, since the females are certainly hanging on the first-time mothers, as an animal does not leave its own that stands before it and show mercy to one that is not its own, so in the first clause too they are certainly exempt from the firstborn, since even if it is not its own, it gave birth to another, and it is merciful only if it has given birth. But really, with regard to “it and its offspring” it is a doubt.
gershom:a14.1: What is “and similarly”? That he compares the first clause to the latter.
gershom:a15.1: Regarding the exemption from the firstborn: since it has already given birth. But really, in the first clause it may show mercy to one that is not its own, and one is not flogged.
rashi:a13.1: Trailing after a ewe: attached behind it, and it nurses it.
rashi:a13.2: Exempt from the firstborn: the one that comes after it is not a firstborn.
rashi:a13.3: Until he comes and instructs righteousness to you: until Elijah comes and instructs whether it is permitted or forbidden.
tosafot:a13.1: Saw a pig that was trailing after a ewe: It is somewhat difficult [to say] that he chose a pig and not a camel because he holds like Rabbi Shimon, who forbids a kelut [an animal with uncloven hooves] born from a kosher animal, so that even if it were known to be the ewe’s offspring it would be forbidden to eat. But we can say that since he chose a ewe, which is a small animal, he chose a pig [likewise small]. Alternatively, he preferred to state his teaching in a way that holds according to everyone.
gershom:a16.1: Trailing after a ewe. And “instructs righteousness”: the Messiah.
rashi:a14.1: Like Rabbi Shimon: it is not merciful to one that is not its own. And this pig itself is not sacred, since it is a look-alike [an offspring resembling another species, which is not a firstborn].
rashi:a14.2: And forbidden to eat, like the Rabbis: since we are concerned for mercy. For if it were like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, it would be a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one, which is permitted to eat, as we said in our first chapter (5b).
gershom:a17.1: Exempt from the firstborn: like whom? Like Rabban Shimon, who said it is not merciful; rather, the matter stands in its presumption that it bore it.
gershom:a18.1: And forbidden to eat, like the Rabbis: who say it is merciful even if it has not given birth. For if it were like Rabban Shimon, it would be permitted to eat, since we hold that what emerges from a kosher animal is kosher. [Part of this note is printed twice on Sefaria; we render it once.]
rashi:a15.1: What is “until he comes and instructs”? Since he holds like the Rabbis, who are concerned for mercy, what is “until he comes and instructs”? It is a matter of revealing the facts, that he should tell us whether it is its offspring or not; and “instructing” is said only of a matter of halakha.
rashi:a15.2: Until the matter becomes known: whether it is its offspring or not.
gershom:a19.1: If like the Rabbis, what is “until he comes and instructs”? Since it is merciful, it is certainly obvious to him that it is forbidden to eat, and a doubt about eating does not need the Messiah’s instruction. Rather he should have said: it is forbidden to eat until the matter becomes known to you, whether it is its offspring.
rashi:a16.1: And if you would say he is uncertain, etc.: and this is what he means: “until he comes and instructs” whether the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, and it is permitted to eat, or the Rabbis, and it is forbidden to eat out of doubt, lest it showed it mercy.
gershom:a20.1: Or the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, who said it is not merciful to one that is not its own.
gershom:a21.1: If like the Rabbis, who say it is merciful: that is why he is in doubt, “until he comes and instructs righteousness.”
rashi:a17.1: Actually, it is obvious to him that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon: that it is exempt from the firstborn, since certainly, even if it is not its own, had it not had offspring it would not have shown it mercy.
rashi:a17.2: But he is uncertain whether Rabbi Shimon holds, etc.: and this is “until he comes and instructs righteousness,” and establishes for us the reasoning of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
rashi:a17.3: An animal that has given birth is merciful: and then this one is forbidden to eat. With regard to the firstborn it is exempt, since if it is its own, well and good, and if it is not its own, it had another. But it is forbidden to eat, since one can say it had another offspring that died, and it showed mercy to this one.
rashi:a17.4: Or it is not merciful: and it is permitted to eat, since it is certainly its own.
gershom:a22.1: Actually, it is obvious to him that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon, but he is uncertain whether Rabbi Shimon holds that an animal that has given birth is merciful even to one that is not its own, or not. It is exempt from the firstborn whichever way you look at it: perhaps it is its offspring, and if it is not its offspring, it certainly would not have shown mercy unless it had already given birth. [The printed text is garbled here; an editor’s gloss suggests reading: “But with regard to the prohibition of eating he is uncertain; that is why he said,” etc.] With regard to eating he is uncertain, and that is why he said “until he comes and instructs righteousness.”
gershom:a23.1: And let him be flogged on its account because of “it and its offspring”: he could not say this about the firstborn, since, as we said, it is exempt from the firstborn whichever way you look at it.
rashi:a18.1: Let him teach us a lamb, and being flogged on its account because of “it and its offspring”: and let him say: one saw a lamb attached to a ewe; it is exempt from the firstborn whichever way you look at it, [since] if this one is not its own, it had another that died, and it showed mercy to this one. But for “it and its offspring” one is not flogged until he comes and instructs us the reasoning of Rabban Shimon.
rashi:a18.2: I would say: even if you say that an animal that has given birth is merciful, this applies only to its own species; but the pig is permitted to eat, since it is not merciful to one not of its species, and this one is certainly its offspring.
rashi:b1.1: Aḥai beribbi: a great and distinguished man in his generation.
rashi:b1.2: Let him ask about a lamb: since it is about a lamb that they disagree.
gershom:b1.1: If we say for the firstborn: whether the halakha follows Rabban Shimon, who said the matter stands in its presumptive status and it is exempt, or the Rabbis, the first tanna, and it is obligated.
rashi:b2.1: He asks about the firstborn according to the Rabbis: for according to Rabbi Shimon it is obvious that it is exempt, since even to one of its own species it would not be merciful unless it had given birth, and all the more so to one not of its species. And with regard to eating he asks even according to Rabban Shimon, and all the more so according to the Rabbis.
gershom:b2.1: They said: when he raised the dilemma: Rabbi Aḥai’s dilemma was about one that has given birth, that is, whether we presume, for this pig trailing after it, that it has already given birth or not. For the firstborn, and the same applies to eating, he asked according to the Rabbis: that is, what the Rabbis said, that it is merciful even though it has never given birth, applies when the one nursing is of its own species; but this one, since it is a pig, I would say even the Rabbis agree that it is certainly not merciful unless it bore it. And for eating alone he asked according to Rabban Shimon: what he said, that one that has given birth is merciful to offspring not its own, applies to its own species, a lamb; but to a pig it is certainly not merciful unless it bore it.
rashi:b3.1: Not of its species, no: it is not merciful, and this one is certainly its own, and it is exempt from the firstborn.
rashi:b3.2: Or perhaps it is merciful even to one not of its species: and the one that comes after it is a firstborn out of doubt.
gershom:b3.1: Or perhaps one not of its species: it is also merciful to it even though it did not bear it, since it has already given birth. And for the firstborn there is no need to ask according to Rabban Shimon, since he said it is merciful only if it has already given birth.
rashi:b4.1: If you say, etc.: if he holds that one that has given birth is not merciful, this one is certainly permitted, since it is its offspring. [The question arises] only if you say that one that has given birth is merciful, and the reason he exempts it from the firstborn is that if this one is not its own it had another; but as for this one trailing after it, it is not obvious to us that it is its own. [Perhaps] that applies to its own species, but not to one not of its species, and this pig is certainly its offspring and permitted to eat.
rashi:b5.1: Mishna. He clears space with a cleaver: he clears the hair away from here and from there, at the place where the knife slaughters.
rashi:b5.2: And plucks the hair: to here and to there, at the place of the knife’s cut, because of ḥalada [the knife being covered during slaughter, which disqualifies it]; and we do not say that he is shearing the firstborn.
tosafot:b5.1: In brief: The Gemara [below] says: read “for the cleaver,” that is, for the needs of the cleaver, which implies that it is usual to slaughter with a cleaver, since it does not say “with a knife.” This is puzzling, since in Pesaḥim (70a) it does not seem so: regarding a knife found on the fourteenth [of Nisan], one slaughters with it at once, but a cleaver must be immersed again, because a knife is fit for slaughtering the Paschal offering and was presumably immersed from the thirteenth, while a cleaver is not fit for the Paschal offering, since it involves breaking a bone. Tosafot explains that the mishna mentions a cleaver because it needs more clearing of space than a knife. This is not as Rashi explained, that the clearing is because of ḥalada: if so, it should have mentioned a knife, where there is more concern for ḥalada; and furthermore, whether one may slaughter under entangled wool is an unresolved dilemma in the second chapter of Ḥullin (30b). Rather, it is usual to clear space for a cleaver to make cutting and slaughtering easier, since a cleaver does not cut easily without it. For the same reason the mishna mentions a firstborn and not consecrated animals in general: consecrated animals are slaughtered in the Temple courtyard, where knives are ready and no clearing is needed. Alternatively, it mentions a firstborn because it applies nowadays, and its wool is usually long, since one keeps it until it gets a blemish, as in the mishna (Bekhorot 35a) about an old male sheep with dangling hair, so it needs more clearing than lambs; and also because the prohibition “you shall not shear” is written about the firstborn. gershom:b4.1: He clears space for the cleaver with which he slaughters: he plucks and cuts some of the wool from here and from there, to make room for the slaughter.
rashi:b5.3: Provided he does not move it: so that people will not say he is shearing sacred animals; rather he leaves it entangled with the wool on either side.
gershom:b5.1: Provided that he does not move it: the wool, from its place on the one [side]; in this way it is not considered shearing.
rashi:b5.4: To see a blemish: to show it to a Sage.
rashi:b6.1: Gemara. The parallel case on a Festival: with a non-sacred animal, for the sake of slaughter, may one do so or not?
rashi:b6.2: Is not shearing: and with a firstborn it is shearing that is forbidden, as it is written: “And you shall not shear” (Deuteronomy 15:19).
rashi:b7.1: Unintentional: he does not intend to pluck, but only clears it away and pulls it this way and that; if it is plucked, it is plucked.
tosafot:b7.1: In brief: The mishna’s “plucks” does not mean intentional plucking; rather he clears space, and if hair is plucked, it is plucked. Yet if the reason were that plucking is not shearing, he could pluck intentionally. Question: then what is there to ask about a Festival? If intentional, it is obviously forbidden; if unintentional, obviously permitted. And if the question is whether an unintentional act is permitted on a Festival, they could have asked about the mishna itself, without a Festival: does “plucks” mean intentionally, because plucking is not shearing, or unintentionally (and not an inevitable result [pesik reisha]), because plucking is shearing? Answer: even if plucking is not shearing, intentional plucking, or an inevitable result, is forbidden by rabbinic law, a decree on account of shearing; so the mishna’s “plucks” is always unintentional and not inevitable, and for a firstborn there is nothing to ask in the plain sense of the mishna except about flogging. The question about a Festival is this: perhaps an unintentional act is permitted only for a firstborn, where plucking is not shearing and there is no Torah prohibition, but not on a Festival, where uprooting from its place of growth is a Torah prohibition; or perhaps a firstborn too involves a Torah prohibition, since plucking is shearing, and just as the unintentional act is permitted there, so it is on a Festival. This is proven from what follows: Rav says the parallel case on a Festival is permitted; the Gemara challenges this from Rav’s ruling like Rabbi Yehuda that an unintentional act is forbidden, and answers that plucking is not shearing, and on a Festival it is permitted because it is uprooting from its place of growth in an unusual manner [ke-le’aḥar yad]. (And if one says that if plucking is not shearing the mishna’s “plucks” is intentional, [one answers that] even intentionally it is permitted on a Festival because it is done in an unusual manner.) According to the other version, that Rav holds like Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam but Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam does not hold like Rav, Rav permits the unintentional act for a firstborn because plucking is not shearing, while Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam permits it even if plucking is shearing, since he permits unintentional acts everywhere, as we find with the red heifer. Question: Rav’s ruling “the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam” implies there is no dispute, yet several tannaim hold that an unintentional act is forbidden (below, Bekhorot 33b, on a firstborn seized by blood; the mishna in Kilayim chapter 9; the baraita on dragging in Beitza 23b). Answer: perhaps Rav rules like him because plucking is not shearing, and on that point no one is found to disagree; and also, as explained above, it is called a dispute only when they disagree about the very same matter. One must say so, since Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis disagree about a partner regarding the first of the shearing (Ḥullin 137a), and some hold him obligated, which implies that it is called “the shearing of your flock”; the same would apply to plucking being shearing, unless one distinguishes between plucking and a partner. Question: below, the Gemara brings a proof from the red heifer that Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam permits unintentional acts, answers that the heifer is consecrated for Temple upkeep, challenges from Rabbi Elazar that Temple-upkeep consecrations are forbidden in shearing and labor, answers “by rabbinic law,” and asks: but there is still a rabbinic prohibition! This implies that if an unintentional act is permitted where the prohibition is rabbinic, it is permitted where it is a Torah one too. Answer: the rabbinic prohibition there is unlike plucking that is not shearing, or uprooting in an unusual manner, which are nowhere Torah prohibitions. The heifer involves real shearing, and although by Torah law Temple-upkeep consecrations are not forbidden in shearing and labor, whatever the Rabbis instituted they modeled on Torah law, and they made Temple-upkeep consecrations fully like altar consecrations. Proof: in Ketubot (5b) they asked whether first intercourse is permitted on Shabbat, and if he needs the blood and the opening comes about by itself, the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, since with respect to the opening it is destructive [mekalkel]: evidently Rabbi Yehuda permits an unintentional act that is destructive, even though a destructive act alone carries a rabbinic prohibition. As for Rabbi Yehuda forbidding an unintentional act in dragging, although it is destructive (as shown in Ḥagiga 10a, on digging a pit when one needs only its earth), and forbidding kidur in Beitza (23a), because an unintentional act is like a destructive one with regard to drawing blood: one can distinguish between a mitzva setting and one that is not; alternatively, with dragging he may be fixing, levelling holes on the other side, and with kidur the animal benefits from the drawing of blood, like bloodletting. So too regarding “and likewise he plucks the hair to see the place of the blemish,” [the Gemara asks whether it means] ab initio or after the fact, and concludes ab initio; and from “and likewise” it follows that the first clause too speaks ab initio. This does not mean he may pluck intentionally ab initio, but that what we permitted for slaughter we also permit ab initio to see the blemish; or “after the fact” would mean that if he did it, he should not move it from its place. Explained this way, the whole passage is settled. And if one explains that if plucking is not shearing one may even pluck intentionally, one must say that below, where the parallel case on a Festival is permitted because it is uprooting in an unusual manner, it is permitted even intentionally, since the Sages permitted it so that his slaughter on the Festival would not be spoiled. gershom:b6.1: An unintentional act: with respect to shearing.
rashi:b8.1: Ask Rav Ḥananel: Rav’s disciple, whether he tells you in Rav’s name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
rashi:b8.2: I will resolve it for you: I [will tell you] the reason.
tosafot:b8.1: If he said the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam, I will resolve it for you: And if you ask: why did he care about this? In any case the parallel case on a Festival is permitted, either because it is an unintentional act or because it is uprooting from its place of growth in an unusual manner, as below. One can say: if the halakha did not follow him, but we forbade it for a firstborn, even though plucking is not shearing, because the Sages were stringent and did not permit it for the sake of preparing the slaughter of a firstborn, then likewise they would not permit uprooting in an unusual manner for the sake of preparing slaughter on a Festival.
